title: Mosca Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Mosca wells have a median depth of 80 feet; see local yields, water levels, drilling costs, and buyer risks.
h1: What Mosca Wells Cost, Produce, and Require
intro_html:
Well records within 5 miles of Mosca show a mostly shallow water-well area, but the records include substantial variation. The median reported depth is 80 feet, and the middle half runs from 60 to 108 feet. That does not guarantee a shallow or inexpensive well on a particular parcel.

These records include domestic, stock, irrigation, and monitoring wells. Of 1,608 wells in the Colorado DWR permit records, 874 are recorded as constructed. Before buying land near Mosca, compare nearby completed wells, confirm the intended water use, and have a driller price the actual access and site conditions.

sections.heading: Mosca well depth depends on the local ground
sections.html:
Mosca wells are commonly shallow in the available records. 66% are under 100 feet, while 26% fall between 100 and 300 feet. The middle half of reported depths, from 60 to 108 feet, is the most useful range for an initial drilling conversation.

Still, the record includes wells as deep as 2,563 feet, with 4% deeper than 600 feet. That spread means a median-depth estimate is not a promise. Mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground can change from one parcel to the next, and some permits identify unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers. A driller should review nearby logs, access, casing and grout requirements before giving a firm bid.

sections.heading: Reported Mosca yields are strong, but verify the test
sections.html:
Among the 352 wells reporting a pump yield, the median is 300.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 15.0 to 500.0 gallons per minute. The record shows 86% above 15 gallons per minute, 14% from 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 1% under 1 gallon per minute.

Those figures are not a guaranteed household supply. Many records are irrigation wells, and a pump-yield entry may not match a sustained household test. Ask for the well completion report and pumping information for the specific parcel. An exempt household-use well is generally limited to 35 gallons per minute under Colorado rules, so a high-yield irrigation record should not be treated as the allowable household pumping rate.

sections.heading: Mosca water levels look shallow without a clear decline
sections.html:
Only 93 records report a static water level, so the water-level sample is much smaller than the depth sample. The median static level is 12 feet below ground, with the middle half between 10 and 14 feet. That is a shallow measured water level, but it is not the same as total well depth.

Measurements by decade were 12 feet in the 1980s, 14 feet in the 2010s, and 13 feet in the 2020s. This series does not show a consistent dropping water table. Seasonal conditions, pumping, measurement method, and the small number of reported levels still matter. Have current water levels checked when evaluating a property, especially if irrigation wells operate nearby.

sections.heading: Mosca has a long permit history and several drillers
sections.html:
Permitting in the Mosca area extends from the 1950s through the newest permit year, 2025. The busiest period in these records was the 1970s, with 292 permits, followed by the 1990s with 264. There were 130 permits in the 2020s so far, so recent activity is still present.

The most active listed drillers are Rocky Mountain Waterworks Llc (Phythian, Donald L.) with 97 records, Biggs And Freel (Biggs, Elmer E) with 93, and Nwp Drlg & Consul (Newmyer, Halsey R.) with 67. These names describe permit history, not a recommendation. Confirm current licensing, availability, and whether a contractor will handle the pump, electrical, trenching, and paperwork.

sections.heading: A typical Mosca well starts near $10,000 finished
sections.html:
For Mosca’s mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground, the drilling model uses approximately $50 to $75 per foot. At the local median depth of 80 feet, the drilled hole is estimated at about $4,000 to $6,000. That is only the hole, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at approximately $10,000 to $18,000. The final price can move outside that range if the site requires unusual casing or grout, difficult access, extra trenching, treatment, or a deeper-than-typical hole. Get a written scope that separates drilling from pump installation and site work, and ask what happens if the first hole has inadequate production.

sections.heading: Check water quality, dry-hole risk, and the building site
sections.html:
Low yield is uncommon in the reported sample, but it is not impossible. A small portion of wells report less than 1 gallon per minute, and many wells have no yield entry at all. A buyer should also understand that permit records do not prove water quality. Within about 10 miles are 1 PFAS sampling or contamination site and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. There are 0 historic mine features mapped in that area.

Test an existing well for the intended household use and ask about septic setbacks, well access, flood or drainage conditions, and space for a replacement system. Confirm the DWR permit and permitted use before building. Irrigation, stock, and domestic permits do not automatically provide the same rights or flexibility.

sections.heading: Use nearby records before buying a Mosca lot
sections.html:
Start with wells closest to the parcel, then expand the comparison toward Hooper, Alamosa East, Alamosa, Center, Monte Vista, and Blanca when the local geology and aquifer information are comparable. Look for reported depth, construction details, static level, yield, and permitted use rather than relying on a single neighbor’s experience.

For a new build, make the well location, septic layout, driveway access, electrical route, and house site work together. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be required for some uses. Have the DWR permit reviewed before closing, obtain a drilling estimate based on the actual parcel, and reserve money for a pump system and testing beyond the drilling price.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Mosca, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Mosca is 80 feet. The middle half runs from 60 to 108 feet, and 66% of recorded wells are under 100 feet. Depths vary widely, however: 26% are from 100 to 300 feet, and the deepest record reaches 2,563 feet. Nearby logs are more useful than the median alone.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Mosca?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $50 to $75 per foot. At Mosca’s 80-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $4,000 to $6,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $10,000 to $18,000. Access, casing, grout, deeper drilling, and site conditions can change the final bid.

faq.q: How much water do Mosca wells produce?
faq.a: Of the 352 wells reporting a pump yield, the median is 300.0 gallons per minute, with a middle-half range of 15.0 to 500.0. Irrigation wells make up 56% of the use mix, so these records may overstate what a household needs or can pump. Request the specific well’s completion and pumping records before relying on a yield.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Mosca?
faq.a: The permit records do not establish that a well is safe to drink. Test an existing or new household well for the intended use, and ask about nearby environmental concerns. Within about 10 miles, the mapped records include 1 PFAS sampling or contamination site and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. A local water-quality professional can select appropriate tests.

faq.q: Are Mosca wells getting deeper or losing water?
faq.a: The reported static water-level medians were 12 feet in the 1980s, 14 feet in the 2010s, and 13 feet in the 2020s. That small series does not show a consistent decline. Only 93 wells report static levels, though, so it is limited. Check current measurements and nearby pumping conditions before buying or building.
